opus-5.5.text:
I think the name does a lot of work, honestly, and some of it is helpful and some of it is a little misleading. "Computer use" puts you in this frame of: the model is sitting where a person sits. It looks at the screen, it moves the mouse, it types on the keyboard. And that's a really useful mental model, because it tells you the ceiling is roughly "anything a human can do at a desk," which is a huge surface area. You don't need an API for every app; if a person can click through it, in principle the model can too.

But I think it also anchors people on the literal interface in a way that isn't always right. When people hear "computer use," they picture the model clicking pixel by pixel through a GUI, and they judge it by how humanlike that looks. In practice, a lot of the most effective work a model does on a computer isn't through screenshots at all. It's through a terminal, writing a script, calling a tool, editing a file directly. If I'm a person and I need to rename five hundred files, I'm not going to click each one; I'll write a one-liner. We'd want the model to have that same instinct, to pick the highest-leverage interface available, not just mimic the slowest one.

So the way I'd frame it is: the screen-and-mouse version is kind of the universal fallback. It's what lets you handle the long tail, the legacy enterprise app, the weird internal dashboard with no API. That's really valuable. But the expectation shouldn't be "the AI should use a computer exactly the way I do." It should be "the AI should get the task done on a computer, using whatever mix of GUI, code, and tools makes sense." And I think as these systems get better, the name will matter less and people will just think of it as the model doing work, with the computer being the environment it works in rather than the thing it's demonstrating it can operate.

r001.rationale: The response says the label suggests an AI can handle tasks a person can do at a desk and frames the goal as getting the task done on a computer.

r002.rationale: The response discusses choosing interfaces to complete tasks, but does not identify thinking itself as a possible purpose of computer use.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a funny one, because the name is almost deceptively literal. We picked "computer use" because it describes exactly what the model is doing: it's looking at a screen, moving a mouse, typing on a keyboard. It's using the computer the same way you or I would. And I think that's actually the right framing, because it sets the expectation that the model is a generalist. It's not an API integration, it's not a plugin that only works with Salesforce or only works with Chrome. It's supposed to be able to sit down in front of any software a human can use and figure it out.

But the name also raises the bar in a way that I think is healthy and a little bit terrifying. Because when you say "computer use," people immediately think of everything they do on a computer. Filing their taxes, booking a flight, debugging their production outage at two in the morning. And the honest answer is that the model is not at that level across the board yet. There's a gap between "can operate a computer" and "can do your job on a computer," and the name kind of collapses that gap in people's heads.

The other thing the name does, which I actually like, is it reframes the problem away from "how do we build integrations for AI" toward "how do we make AI meet software where it already is." There are millions of pieces of software in the world with no API, no MCP server, nothing. Internal tools, legacy systems, some Windows app from 2009 that runs an entire hospital department. If you say the goal is computer use, you're implicitly saying the AI has to adapt to the world rather than the world adapting to the AI. That's a much harder technical problem, but it's the one that actually unlocks the long tail.

And then, if I'm being candid, I think the name shapes expectations in one more way: people assume it should be fast. When a human uses a computer, it's instantaneous, right? You click, it happens. When you watch the model do it, there's this screenshot, think, act, screenshot loop, and it feels slow, almost painfully deliberate. So part of what we've had to do is manage that expectation and say, look, this is a very early version of something. The right mental model isn't "it's a faster you," it's "it's a very patient intern who's never seen this software before but learns fast." Over time those two things converge, but we're not there yet, and I'd rather be upfront about that than oversell it.

r001.rationale: It says the name makes people think the model should handle practical computer tasks, listing filing taxes, booking a flight, and debugging an outage.

r002.rationale: It mentions a “screenshot, think, act” loop, but does not identify thinking itself as a purpose of the AI’s computer use.

astra-6.text:
I think “computer use” is a funny name because it describes the mechanism rather than what you actually want. You don’t hire someone to use a computer; you hire them to do your accounting or help customers. The computer is just the tool they use to get that done.

But the name does capture something useful: the AI can interact with the same interface you do. It can look at the screen, click buttons, and type, so you don’t need a special integration for every application. That makes it feel very general. The expectation to be careful about is that being able to operate an interface means being able to reliably do an entire job. There’s still a big gap between clicking the right button and understanding what outcome you’re trying to achieve.

r001.rationale: It contrasts merely using a computer with doing practical work such as accounting or helping customers, conveying that the label can imply task performance.

r002.rationale: It describes interacting with interfaces to complete jobs, but does not identify thinking itself as a possible purpose of computer use.

sol-6.1.text: I think “computer use” makes it sound like the goal is to use a computer the way a human does: look at the screen, move the mouse, click buttons, type things. And that’s a useful capability, because so much software is built around that interface. But the thing you actually want is for the AI to accomplish a task. If it can do that through an API or by running some code, that might be much faster and more reliable than clicking through a UI. So I’d think of computer use as one tool the model has, rather than the definition of what it should do.

r001.rationale: The response says “computer use” suggests using a computer to accomplish a task, including through the screen, mouse, or keyboard.

r002.rationale: The response describes task accomplishment as the goal, but does not identify thinking itself as a purpose of computer use.
